## What it is

A lightweight backend that the voice agent calls as its tools. It keeps bookings consistent and asks a route optimizer whether a requested trip fits into a vehicle's schedule. Unlike the agent, it is part of the open benchmark, so anyone can run the same booking tasks against their own agent.

## Why it matters for the testbed

A voice call only counts as a success if the system ends up with the right booking. The API gives every simulated call a ground truth to check against: the evaluator compares the final booking with the caller's goal. Because the solver says yes or no to a trip, an agent that mishears a pickup time can produce a booking that is feasible but wrong, which is exactly the failure the testbed is built to measure.

## Endpoints (planned)

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `request_trip` | Propose a ride: pickup, drop-off, time window, passengers |
| `check_feasibility` | Ask the optimizer whether and where the trip can be inserted |
| `confirm` | Commit a feasible trip to a vehicle schedule |
| `modify` | Change time, stops or passenger count on an existing booking |
| `cancel` | Release the booking and update the schedule |

## Data and solver

Transit context comes from the TTC's GTFS and GTFS-Realtime feeds on Toronto Open Data. Demand comes from public dial-a-ride benchmark instances, such as Cordeau's. The solver is pluggable: version 1 uses a simple insertion heuristic or OR-Tools, and an adaptive large neighbourhood search (ALNS) solver can be swapped in later without changing the API.

## Release checklist

- [ ] Endpoints running against a simple solver
- [ ] Public data loaded: GTFS stops plus one dial-a-ride instance
- [ ] Text-mode agent completes one booking end to end
- [ ] API reference and a one-command local setup
